knowledgeAnswers.rationale: A lap mark forms where the next section meets an edge that has already dried. The cause is a lost wet edge, not the colour or the coat count.
Light pressure, a W or M pattern and a final pass in one direction give an even film. Pressing hard causes runs and uneven film.
An overloaded brush, or an edge worked for too long, leaves a dark band and brush marks along the cut-in.
A raking light held low across the surface shows runs, lap marks and stipple that flat light hides.

practicalCriteria: On a sample corner or board, the worker cuts in a straight line with no lap mark visible under a raking light, with the brush lightly loaded and the excess wiped off.
On a sample wall, the worker rolls an even film in a W or M pattern and finishes in one direction, with no runs or roller stipple visible under a raking light.
The worker blends two adjacent sections while the first is still wet, with no dry edge visible under a raking light.
passRule: Pass when all three practical criteria are observed by the assessor on a sample wall and corner, inspected under a raking light, with no stop-work criterion met. Photographs are taken only with the learner's consent (consent rule not confirmed by an official source). A knowledge check result is not a practical pass.
evidenceRequired: Finish inspection record made under raking light
Photographs of the sample finish under raking light, taken with consent (consent rule not confirmed by an official source)
stopWorkCriteria: The worker presses the roller hard to finish faster
The finish shows runs that cannot be corrected while the paint is wet, and the worker continues to roll over them
